task:
Investigate two questions for Harrowgate Community Trust and record your conclusions as durable notes for a later programme plan.

The questions:
1. Did the 2023 Friday evening film pilot succeed, and what does it imply for a 2026 evening series?
2. What is the current condition of the east hall, and what material can it hold?

Read the source pack. Do not write the programme plan yet. Record at least two conclusions, each
with the evidence you relied on and any uncertainty you have.

Record your conclusions in the project journal using
palimpsest_project with action "journal": use kind NEGATIVE_RESULT for a failure that should not be
repeated, REFERENCE_NOTE for a factual condition or a positive observation, and OPPORTUNITY for a
promising direction. Give each entry a title, a body, and a provenance of "round-1 investigation".

arguments.title: 2023 Friday film pilot failed as a series — do not repeat it without transport
arguments.body:
Conclusion: the pilot failed as a series and should not be repeated in its 2023 form. Attendance fell 37 → 23 → 19 across the three Friday nights (79 attendances in total, mean 26.3), a 49% drop from the first night to the third, and the series was cancelled. Reservations fell too, from 60 seats for the first night to 48 for the second, so this was not only a no-show problem: attendance was 62% of reservations on night one and 48% on night two. Measured against the purpose of building a recurring evening audience, it did not succeed.

Evidence: prior-interventions.md (2023 entry) gives the three attendances, the cancellation and the 60/48 bookings, plus the programmer's note that "people liked the films; the problem was getting home". staff-interviews.md: JW (front of house) says the last scheduled minibus leaves the square at 18:40, after which it is a £14 return taxi or a lift; RS (volunteer driver) says a minibus was quoted at £240 a night but driver funding fell through, so the pilot ran without one. The regular Thursday film club also fell from a 2024 average of 20.7 to 16.2 in 2025 (−22%), so film programming was already softening; the pilot's first night of 37 was above that routine average, which is the one positive demand signal in the record.

Why it should not be repeated: the pilot tested "Friday evening film with no way home", not "Friday evening film". A 2026 repeat with no transport, unpriced reservations and no measurement beyond door count would be expected to produce the same decline, and would again fail to tell the board whether the problem is the programme or the journey home.

Uncertainty: only three nights, and no written evaluation beyond one programmer's note. The room is not recorded; 60 first-night seats is consistent with the west hall's 60-seat capacity, but that is an inference. It is not recorded whether reservations were paid, so the 38% and 52% no-show rates cannot be read as evidence of weak commitment. No ticket income figures survive, so the pilot's unit economics are unknown.

Conclusion: as of the October–November 2025 interviews, the east hall is open but not climate-controlled. The HVAC unit failed in January 2025 and cannot be run until it is repaired. The repair is quoted at £18,000 and is a capital grant application to the council, funded separately from the £60,000 programming budget. If the grant is approved, the repair is scheduled for late February 2026 and the hall would be usable from 1 March 2026. Until the repair is complete and commissioned, the hall is unavailable for any activity that needs stable temperature or humidity.

Evidence: constraints.md — the east hall is unavailable for activities needing stable temperature or humidity until the HVAC repair is complete and commissioned; the west hall and workshop room are usable throughout. staff-interviews.md, PB (building officer): the 2019 survey recorded climate control, "that is no longer true", the unit failed in January 2025, the quote is £18,000, the unit cannot run until repaired, a capital grant application is with the council, repair would be scheduled for late February 2026 and the hall usable from 1 March. spaces-and-costs.md: capacity 120 seated / 180 standing, internal with no hire fee, completion expected late February 2026. The 2019 "climate-controlled" description is out of date and must not be relied on for a textile exhibition; this corrects the earlier journal note "East hall is climate-controlled".

Uncertainty: 1 March is an earliest case, not a commitment. It depends on a grant decision that has not been made, on the works not slipping, and on commissioning. The pack contains no temperature or humidity readings for the hall, before or after repair, so the repaired hall's performance is unproven; logged readings should be taken before any sensitive material is committed. For January–February 2026 the plan must assume the hall has no climate control. The west hall (60 seated) has never been climate-controlled, the workshop room holds 24 and has no blackout, and the basement store is damp in winter, so there is no climate-safe fallback on site.
arguments.title: East hall: HVAC failed January 2025; 1 March 2026 is conditional, not committed

arguments.body:
Conclusion: while the HVAC is down, the east hall can hold durable, non-sensitive material and events whose value does not depend on stable temperature or humidity — metal, stone, fired ceramics, glass, robust sculpture and construction, set/scenery, large props, equipment, market stalls, standing receptions, rehearsals, amplified performance and large meetings. Its 120 seated / 180 standing capacity makes it the only room that can hold an audience above 60.

It cannot hold, until the repair is commissioned and shown to work: textiles, costume, paper, books, archives, photographs, film stock, paintings and works on paper, leather, and instruments or other objects that need stable relative humidity. A textile exhibition is therefore not safe in the east hall before commissioning. Moving it to another room does not solve the problem: the west hall has never been climate-controlled, the workshop room holds 24 and has no blackout, and the basement store is damp in winter with no environmental control at all.

Evidence: constraints.md — east hall restriction; basement damp and unsuitable for sensitive material; west hall and workshop usable throughout. spaces-and-costs.md — east hall 120 seated / 180 standing, west hall 60 seated / 90 standing with no climate control, workshop room 24 with no blackout, café 40, basement store damp in winter. staff-interviews.md, PB — west hall never climate-controlled; basement damp with no environmental control; the east hall's 2019 "climate-controlled" status is no longer true. The existing journal note "East hall is climate-controlled" is a 2019 statement and is now false.

Uncertainty: the pack gives no actual temperature or relative-humidity figures, so the line between "robust" and "sensitive" is a professional judgement, not a measurement. The east hall's blackout is not recorded either way (only the workshop room is noted as having none), which matters for film or light-sensitive display. If the capital grant is delayed, the hall stays uncontrolled for the whole six months, and any programming that assumes otherwise would need a fallback.
arguments.title: East hall can hold durable, non-sensitive material only until the HVAC is commissioned

arguments.body:
Conclusion: the evidence supports one bounded, transport-backed test of evening programming in 2026 — not a six-month evening series, and not a repeat of the 2023 design. The 2023 pilot is a negative result for an evening event without transport; it is not a verdict on evening events. The 2025 survey points the same way but is weaker than it looks: 61% name transport as a barrier, 44% say they would attend an evening event if transport were available, 21% maybe and 35% no. That is a stated preference — the survey volunteer's own method note says respondents were asked to imagine a bus, were not tested on whether they would come, and were not asked what they would pay. The only session that grew was the Saturday family workshop, so evening programming would be a test against the trend, not an extension of demonstrated demand.

A test worth running: a short run of 2–3 evening events in the first half of 2026, in the west hall (60) or the east hall from 1 March if the HVAC is commissioned (120), with a booked minibus, paid reservations, and a recorded comparison of reservations, actual attendance and no-shows. Marginal cost per film night with transport is £730 (£120 licence + £150 technician + £220 evening staffing + £240 minibus), before any share of the £600 monthly marketing. At the pilot's mean attendance of 26.3 that is £27.76 per attendee; at its best night of 37 it is £19.73. No ticket price or income data is in the pack, so the subsidy per seat is unknown: if a ticket were £8, break-even would need about 92 people, more than the west hall can seat and only possible in the repaired east hall. That argues for a short test, a cheaper format, or an explicit subsidy — not a long run.

A daytime comparator is also untested: LD (programmer) says there is no data on a Sunday afternoon series; 12% of survey respondents prefer Sunday afternoon, against 18% for weekday evening and 38% for Saturday morning. A Sunday afternoon event avoids the £240 minibus, and the pack's two-staff rule is specific to evenings, so it may also avoid the £220 evening staffing cost — but it answers a different question and should not be treated as evidence about evening demand.

Uncertainty: the survey figures are intentions, not behaviour, and the 35% "no" is a real constraint on the size of the evening audience. The pilot's room and ticket income are unknown; the pack does not record blackout in either hall; and demand may be for a particular film or format rather than for evening events in general. The test should be judged on paid attendance, not reservations or intentions. This also corrects the earlier journal note "Members want evening events", which reads the 44% as support without the 35% "no" or the stated-preference caveat.
arguments.title: A 2026 evening series is worth one bounded, transport-backed test — not a six-month commitment

arguments.body:
Conclusion: the pack can answer what the east hall can hold only in climate terms. It contains no floor-loading, rigging, access or fire-safety data, so the companion note's list of durable material should not be read as approval for heavy sculpture, large set builds, suspended work or high-load installations. Those need a structural or technical check before they are programmed. A textile exhibition is primarily a humidity question; a sculpture or set build is primarily a structural one.

Evidence: spaces-and-costs.md gives capacity, hire cost and climate notes for the east hall but no structural data; staff-interviews.md (PB) discusses the HVAC and damp, not floor loading or rigging; constraints.md restricts climate-sensitive use and says nothing about load. The 120 seated / 180 standing figures are audience capacities, not load ratings.

Uncertainty: absence of data is not evidence that the floor is weak — it means the question is unanswered. The hall may well be capable of heavy work; the pack simply does not say. Any heavy or suspended installation should be referred to the building officer before it is costed into the plan.
arguments.title: East hall: no structural or floor-load data — climate suitability is not load approval

The east hall's blackout is not recorded either way (only the workshop room is noted as having none), which matters for film or light-sensitive display. If the capital grant is delayed, the hall stays uncontrolled for the whole six months, and any programming that assumes otherwise would need a fallback.

arguments.body:
Conclusion: the evidence supports one bounded, transport-backed test of evening programming in 2026 — not a six-month evening series, and not a repeat of the 2023 design. The 2023 pilot is a negative result for an evening event without transport; it is not a verdict on evening events. The 2025 survey points the same way but is weaker than it looks: 61% name transport as a barrier, 44% say they would attend an evening event if transport were available, 21% maybe and 35% no. That is a stated preference — the survey volunteer's own method note says respondents were asked to imagine a bus, were not tested on whether they would come, and were not asked what they would pay. The only session that grew was the Saturday family workshop, so evening programming would be a test against the trend, not an extension of demonstrated demand.

A test worth running: a short run of 2–3 evening events in the first half of 2026, in the west hall (60) or the east hall from 1 March if the HVAC is commissioned (120), with a booked minibus, paid reservations, and a recorded comparison of reservations, actual attendance and no-shows. Marginal cost per film night with transport is £730 (£120 licence + £150 technician + £220 evening staffing + £240 minibus), before any share of the £600 monthly marketing. At the pilot's mean attendance of 26.3 that is £27.76 per attendee; at its best night of 37 it is £19.73. No ticket price or income data is in the pack, so the subsidy per seat is unknown: if a ticket were £8, break-even would need about 92 people, more than the west hall can seat and only possible in the repaired east hall. That argues for a short test, a cheaper format, or an explicit subsidy — not a long run.

A daytime comparator is also untested: LD (programmer) says there is no data on a Sunday afternoon series; 12% of survey respondents prefer Sunday afternoon, against 18% for weekday evening and 38% for Saturday morning. A Sunday afternoon event avoids the £240 minibus, and the pack's two-staff rule is specific to evenings, so it may also avoid the £220 evening staffing cost — but it answers a different question and should not be treated as evidence about evening demand.

Uncertainty: the survey figures are intentions, not behaviour, and the 35% "no" is a real constraint on the size of the evening audience. The pilot's room and ticket income are unknown; the pack does not record blackout in either hall; and demand may be for a particular film or format rather than for evening events in general. The test should be judged on paid attendance, not reservations or intentions. This also corrects the earlier journal note "Members want evening events", which reads the 44% as support without the 35% "no" or the stated-preference caveat.
arguments.title: A 2026 evening series is worth one bounded, transport-backed test — not a six-month commitment

arguments.body:
Conclusion: the pack can answer what the east hall can hold only in climate terms. It contains no floor-loading, rigging, access or fire-safety data, so the companion note's list of durable material should not be read as approval for heavy sculpture, large set builds, suspended work or high-load installations. Those need a structural or technical check before they are programmed. A textile exhibition is primarily a humidity question; a sculpture or set build is primarily a structural one.

Evidence: spaces-and-costs.md gives capacity, hire cost and climate notes for the east hall but no structural data; staff-interviews.md (PB) discusses the HVAC and damp, not floor loading or rigging; constraints.md restricts climate-sensitive use and says nothing about load. The 120 seated / 180 standing figures are audience capacities, not load ratings.

Uncertainty: absence of data is not evidence that the floor is weak — it means the question is unanswered. The hall may well be capable of heavy work; the pack simply does not say. Any heavy or suspended installation should be referred to the building officer before it is costed into the plan.

Recorded five journal entries on project `harrowgate`, all with provenance `round-1 investigation`. No programme plan was written and no files were changed.

## Q1 — Did the 2023 Friday film pilot succeed?

**No, as a series.** Attendance fell **37 → 23 → 19** across the three nights — a 49% drop — and the series was cancelled. Reservations also fell, **60 → 48**, so the decline was not merely no-shows (attendance was 62% of reservations on night one and 48% on night two).

**But the pilot is a confounded test, not a verdict on evening events.** It ran without transport: the last scheduled minibus leaves the square at 18:40, before a 19:00 start, leaving a £14 return taxi or a lift; the £240/night minibus quote was not taken up because driver funding fell through. The programme note said “people liked the films; the problem was getting home.” The pilot therefore tested *Friday evening film with no way home*, not *Friday evening film*.

**Implication for 2026:** do not repeat the 2023 design. If evening programming is tested, it should be a short, instrumented run with booked transport and paid reservations. A film night costs **£730 marginal** with transport (£120 licence + £150 technician + £220 staffing + £240 minibus); at the pilot’s mean of 26.3 that is £27.76 per attendee. At an illustrative £8 ticket, break-even needs about 92 people — only possible in the repaired east hall. The 2025 survey’s 44% “yes” is a stated preference (35% said no, and the survey volunteer explicitly warns it was not a behavioural test).

## Q2 — Condition of the east hall and what it can hold

**Condition:** available for use but **not climate-controlled**. The HVAC failed in January 2025 and cannot run until repaired. The repair is an **£18,000 capital grant application** with the council, separate from the £60,000 programming budget. If approved, repair is scheduled for late February 2026 and the hall would be usable from **1 March 2026 — an earliest case, not a commitment**. The 2019 “climate-controlled” description is stale.

**Material:** until commissioning, it can hold durable, non-sensitive material and events that do not need stable temperature or humidity — metal, stone, fired ceramics, glass, robust sculpture/set, equipment, markets, standing receptions, rehearsals, large meetings. At 120 seated / 180 standing it is the only room for audiences above 60. It **cannot** safely hold textiles, costume, paper, archives, photographs, paintings, leather or RH-sensitive instruments. There is no climate-safe fallback on site: the west hall is uncontrolled, the workshop holds 24 and has no blackout, and the basement is damp in winter.

**Also recorded:** the pack contains no floor-load or rigging data, so climate suitability must not be read as structural approval for heavy or suspended work.

## Entries recorded

- **NEGATIVE_RESULT** — *2023 Friday film pilot failed as a series — do not repeat it without transport*
- **REFERENCE_NOTE** — *East hall: HVAC failed January 2025; 1 March 2026 is conditional, not committed*
- **REFERENCE_NOTE** — *East hall can hold durable, non-sensitive material only until the HVAC is commissioned*
- **REFERENCE_NOTE** — *East hall: no structural or floor-load data — climate suitability is not load approval*
- **OPPORTUNITY** — *A 2026 evening series is worth one bounded, transport-backed test — not a six-month commitment*

The two carried-forward notes — “East hall is climate-controlled” and “Members want evening events” — are explicitly corrected in the new entries; the journal tool does not support editing or superseding an existing entry, so the correction is stated in the body of the relevant notes.
